claims.text: A single-phase, chemically disordered fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti solid solution can be formed by rapid solidification or homogenization.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti has a suppressed orbital moment and coercivity below 100 Oe.
Adjusting Ti concentration and annealing will precipitate a secondary phase while retaining an fcc matrix.
The precipitate can be a Ti-rich ordered BCC phase, such as B2, TiFe, TiNi, or sigma.
Prolonged annealing at 600–800 K will permit phase decomposition in Fe-Co-Ni-Ti.
The annealing treatment can preserve the fcc matrix while producing nano-sized secondary-phase precipitates.
Nano-sized precipitates maximize interfacial area.
The fcc matrix and Ti-rich BCC secondary phase will form coherent or semi-coherent interfaces.
The fcc/BCC interfaces act as domain-wall pinning sites.
The interfaces modify the local electronic structure and restore an orbital-moment contribution.
Local strain fields and chemical segregation disrupt the uniform fcc lattice and reduce orbital-moment suppression.
Interfacial exchange coupling between the fcc matrix and BCC precipitates enhances magnetic anisotropy.
Interfacial exchange coupling and domain-wall pinning will raise coercivity above 100 Oe.
The dual-phase alloy will retain a Curie temperature above 300 K.
The dual-phase alloy will show a magnetically harder hysteresis loop than the single-phase baseline.
A single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti baseline has high ductility.
A continuous secondary-phase network would degrade mechanical properties.
Reducing the ferromagnetic fcc volume fraction below a critical threshold would prevent retention of a high Curie temperature.
Excessive Ti content can transform the alloy into a fully BCC structure.
Prolonged annealing may cause precipitate coarsening or excessive grain growth.

contradictions.description: The design specifies an ordered BCC secondary phase but lists sigma phase as an example. Sigma is a distinct non-BCC structure, so it is inconsistent with the stated BCC phase constraint.
